study.title: Galatians 3 The promise comes by faith, not by the Law
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul corrects the Galathas because they have been diverted from the gospel of faith in Christ and shows, through Abraham, the Law and the promise, that justification and inheritance come through faith, not the works of the Law. He contrasts the provisional function of the Law with the centrality of Christ, who rescues from the curse, fulfills the promise to Abraham and gathers Jews and Gentiles into one family of God.

outline.title: The Christian experience of the gallates did not come from the Law
outline.explanation: Paul begins with a strong rebuke: they received the Spirit and saw the action of God not by observance of the Law, but by the preaching of faith. The argument appeals to their own experience to show the inconsistency of abandoning the beginning in the Spirit and trying to end by the flesh.

outline.title: Abraham, the faith and the deliverance of the curse
outline.explanation: Paul proves that God's pattern has always been faith: Abraham believed and was accepted as righteous, and Scripture already announced that the Gentiles would be blessed in him. In contrast, whoever stands under the Law enters the sphere of the curse, because the Law requires integral obedience; however, Christ took the curse upon himself to bring Abraham's blessing and the promise of the Spirit to those who believe.

outline.title: The promise is earlier and superior to the Law
outline.explanation: Paul uses the example of a human pact to show that a confirmed covenant is not annulled later. The promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, which he identifies in Christ; the Law, came centuries later, does not revoke the promise. His function was provisional: to expose transgressions, to serve as mediation and to lead the people to Christ, as a tutor who prepares for the maturity of faith.

outline.title: Children, clothed with Christ and heirs of promise
outline.explanation: Now Paul applies everything to believers: by faith in Christ Jesus, they are children of God, clothed with Christ by baptism and united in a new reality where ethnic, social and gender distinctions do not define status before God. Belonging to Christ means belonging to Abraham's offspring and becoming heir according to the promise.

study.context: Paul writes to churches of Galatia that were being pressured by teachers to add observance of the Law of Moses, especially Jewish identity signs, as a requirement to fully belong to God's people. The chapter responds to this crisis by explaining that the gospel already offered, in Christ, what the promise to Abraham anticipated: acceptance before God, blessing and inheritance.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that justification is received by faith and not by the observance of the Law; therefore, the basis of the saving relationship with God is Christ, not human performance. The promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and reaches the Gentiles without them having to become Jews. The Law is not treated as error, but as a temporary and pedagogical instrument: it reveals sin, guards the people and leads it to Christ. In Christ, the identity of God's people is defined by union with him, not by ethnic boundaries, social status or sex distinctions. Thus, the Abrahamic inheritance is received as a gift of grace, not as a wage for works.

scholarViews.insight: Paul contrasts the spiritual experience of the gallates with that of Abraham to show that both they and the patriarch were accepted before God in the same way: by faith, not by the Law.
Paul uses the promise given to Abraham to show that justification does not come by the Law; the inheritance is given by promise, and the later Law does not annul this covenant.

The receiving of the Spirit may include the spiritual gifts and also the spirit of adoption; in both cases, Paul uses the experience of the Galathas to prove that God attained them by faith and not by the Law.

questions: In what areas are we tempted to begin in the Spirit and then want to support the Christian life by merely human effort?
How does the identification of Christ as Abraham's offspring correct our way of understanding who belongs to God's people?
What concrete signs show in our community that the inheritance received is the fruit of the promise and not merit?
study.practice: Examine whether you have sought security before God in religious performance, external discipline, or comparison with others. Reaffirm daily that his acceptance comes from Christ and responds to it with gratitude, obedience and trust, not with spiritual self-promotion. In the Christian community, treat brothers of different backgrounds as equally heirs of promise, avoiding any pride of group, class or tradition.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not discuss in detail all verses, so some applications were made by synthesis of the chapter argument. In verse 20, there is recognized interpretive difficulty, but the notes do not require a conclusive position, so the study only records its function in Paul's reasoning. There is also textual variation pointed out by Adam Clarke at 3:1; as this does not alter the central teaching of the chapter, it was only mentioned in general.
